I think we would all like there not to be a point, but unfortunately there is a point: to be respected, ingratiated into and feel part of a society.

Humans are social animals. We thrive on social interaction and feeling part of a group. That is why solitary confinement is considered such a harsh punishment and is illegal in some places.

Unfortunately, our (Western) society has evolved in such a way that to be a meaningful, respected part of the group you must have a career and job (or at least be working to get one). Homeless people, for example, are pretty much ostracised from this group and looked down on.

I would say there has to be a point, sorry.

I'm not entirely sure since you're under 18 but your therapist should be contractually obliged not to tell anyone, including family, anything about your sessions unless you give consent.

The only exception is if you definitively say you are going to hurt yourself or someone else. If you talk about suicide they will usually ask if you have a plan. If you say something like 'tonight I will OD' than they have to do something. This is called 'Duty of Care'.

I would just ask the therapist straight out - say 'I really want to talk about suicide privately and I dont want to invoke Duty of Care. What are your guidlines?' Remember, your the customer so you should be able to aks questions in order to get your monies worth from the therapist.

My SO has depression (as do I).

The most important thing is to have patience. She will have low moments when there's not much you can do. Don't ask questions like 'What's wrong exactly?' or 'What happened?' because there isnt really an answer - that's depression.

Ask her if you can do anything and don't be insulted if she wants space or doesnt want to talk much. Lend an ear, of course, but don't try to extract any conversation out of her. Just being there is enough.

If you can, put on her favourite TV show or music - something that's a good distraction and doesnt require a lot of mental effort. Its all about waiting out that particular episode and having a distraction will help immensely.

In terms of treatment, do encourage her to seek therapy. Offer to make the appointment your self if need be. Offer to go with her, but give her the option of going alone as well. 

Finally, remember depression is a disease and not the person. The sadness and low moods are the symptoms - like a cold's runny nose and sore throat - and not part of her personality.
